items.stem: A company runs a web application on four Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer in one AWS Region. The VPC has subnets across multiple Availability Zones, but all four instances run in the same Availability Zone. Last month, a failure in that Availability Zone stopped the application for two hours. The application must be highly available and must keep serving requests if one Availability Zone fails. What should a solutions architect do?
keywords: all four instances run in the same Availability Zone
keep serving requests if one Availability Zone fails

options.text: Replace the four instances with two larger instances in the same Availability Zone, so that each instance can carry the whole load.
options.why: Larger instances add capacity, not zones: if that zone fails, [none of your EC2 instances would be available](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-single-az-failure-takes-all-instances).
options.misconception: believes that bigger instances survive the failure of their Availability Zone

options.text: Launch the instances across subnets in two Availability Zones, and register the instances in both zones with the load balancer.
options.why: AWS says to run production workloads in [at least two Availability Zones (AZs) in a Region](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-production-at-least-two-azs), so a zone failure leaves the other zone serving.

options.text: Take daily snapshots of the instance volumes, and restore the instances from the snapshots in another Availability Zone after a failure.
options.why: A snapshot is a backup, not a running copy, so the application stays down while someone restores the instances.
options.misconception: treats a backup as a highly available design

options.text: Create an Auto Scaling group in the current Availability Zone that replaces each unhealthy instance with a new instance in that zone.
options.why: The group replaces instances inside the same zone, and when that zone fails, [none of your EC2 instances would be available](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-single-az-failure-takes-all-instances).

items.explanation: The stem names one failure: the loss of one Availability Zone. When every instance runs in that zone, [none of your EC2 instances would be available](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-single-az-failure-takes-all-instances) after a zone failure. AWS recommends [at least two Availability Zones](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-prod-at-least-two-azs) for production, so the answer spreads the instances across two zones behind the load balancer.
items.takeaway: Find the failure that the stem names, then choose the design that survives exactly that failure.
items.twin: If the stem said "must keep serving requests if the whole Region fails" instead: a design in a second Region, because each Region is [designed to be isolated from the other Regions](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-region-isolated-for-fault-tolerance).
items.say: The stem names a zone failure, so I spread the instances across two Availability Zones.

solvers.stem_only: Spread the instances across at least two Availability Zones (for example an Auto Scaling group over subnets in several zones) and register them all with the existing Application Load Balancer so it routes around a failed zone.

items.stem: A company runs workloads on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets in three Availability Zones of one VPC. Each private subnet has its own route table. The instances download software updates from a vendor's website on the internet, and the traffic volume is small. The instances must not have public IP addresses. If one Availability Zone fails, an interruption of internet access is acceptable. What is the MOST cost-effective solution that meets these requirements?
keywords: an interruption of internet access is acceptable
must not have public IP addresses

options.text: Create one NAT gateway in a public subnet in one Availability Zone, and point the default route of every private route table to that NAT gateway.
options.why: Private subnets reach the internet when you [create a NAT gateway or launch a NAT instance in a public subnet](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-route-from-private-subnet), and here one gateway can serve every zone.

options.text: Create one NAT gateway in a public subnet in each Availability Zone, and point the default route of each private route table to the NAT gateway in its zone.
options.why: One gateway in each zone works, but the stem accepts an interruption, and three gateways cost more than one because the number of gateways is billed.

options.text: Create two NAT gateways in public subnets in each Availability Zone, and point the default route of each private route table to one NAT gateway in its zone.
options.why: It works, but [each NAT gateway is created in a specific Availability Zone and implemented with redundancy in that zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-one-az-redundant-in-zone), so a second one adds cost.
options.misconception: believes that a second NAT gateway in the same zone adds resilience

options.text: Assign a public IP address to each instance, and point the default route of each private route table to the internet gateway of the VPC.
options.why: The stem forbids public IP addresses on the instances, so this design breaks a stated requirement at any price.

items.explanation: Three options give the instances internet access without public IP addresses. The stem accepts an interruption if one zone fails, so the qualifier decides. NAT gateways are [charged depending on the number of NAT gateways you use, duration of usage, and amount of data that you send through the NAT gateways](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-vs-instance-cost), and the traffic is small, so one shared gateway costs least.
items.takeaway: When the stem accepts an interruption, the cheaper design that still meets every requirement wins.
items.twin: If the stem said "Internet access must continue if one Availability Zone fails" instead: one NAT gateway in each zone, because otherwise [resources in the other Availability Zones lose internet access](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-shared-across-azs-loses-internet).
items.say: An interruption is acceptable, so one shared NAT gateway is the cheapest design that works.

solvers.stem_only: Because an outage on zone failure is acceptable and traffic is small, use a single NAT gateway in one public subnet and point all private route tables' default routes to it; per-zone NAT gateways cost more for availability that is not required.

items.stem: A company uses AWS Organizations and has 30 member accounts. Its 200 employees sign in to company applications through the company's existing identity provider. Each employee needs access to a different set of accounts. The security team wants to centrally manage this access from one place, and employees must use temporary credentials in the accounts. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create IAM users with the same names in each member account, and require the employees to rotate the access keys of those users on a schedule.
options.why: [IAM users have long-term credentials such as passwords and access keys](../facts/iam.md#iam-users-have-long-term-credentials-roles-do-not), so rotating the keys does not make the credentials temporary.
options.misconception: believes that a rotated access key is a temporary credential

options.text: Create an IAM role in each member account that trusts the identity provider through SAML federation, and update the roles in every account by hand.
options.why: It works, but the team creates and updates a role in every account by hand, work that IAM Identity Center does for each permission set.

options.text: Connect the identity provider to IAM Identity Center, create permission sets, and assign groups of employees to the accounts that they need.
options.why: IAM Identity Center [creates and manages IAM roles in individual AWS accounts for each permission set](../facts/iam.md#iam-idc-creates-role-per-permission-set), so the team assigns access in one place.

options.text: Create one IAM user in the management account for all employees, share its password, and let the employees switch roles into member accounts.
options.why: One shared user gives every employee the same access, so the employees do not get different sets of accounts.
options.misconception: shares one identity among many people to save setup work

items.explanation: Several options give access, and the qualifier ranks the ones that work. AWS calls IAM Identity Center its [recommended front door into AWS](../facts/iam.md#iam-idc-recommended-front-door-for-workforce) for workforce users. The team connects the existing identity provider once and assigns permission sets, and employees receive role credentials in each account instead of user keys.
items.takeaway: Workforce access to many accounts with the least work: IAM Identity Center with permission sets.
items.twin: If the stem said "an application on Amazon EC2 instances needs access" instead: an IAM role for the instances, because [AWS delivers the temporary credentials of an IAM role to that compute resource](../facts/iam.md#iam-compute-services-receive-role-credentials-no-keys-needed).
items.say: For people in many accounts I'd use IAM Identity Center with permission sets, not users in each account.

solvers.stem_only: Use IAM Identity Center connected to the existing external identity provider, define permission sets, and assign users or groups to the accounts they need; access uses short-term credentials and is managed centrally.

items.stem: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets in two Availability Zones. The instances currently send large uploads to an Amazon S3 bucket in the same AWS Region through one NAT gateway. The uploads come only from the instances in the VPC. The uploads must reach Amazon S3 privately, and the company wants to reduce the NAT gateway data processing charges. What is the MOST cost-effective solution that meets these requirements?
keywords: come only from the instances in the VPC

options.text: Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3, and add a route to the endpoint in the route table of each private subnet.
options.why: [There are no data processing or hourly charges for using Gateway Type VPC endpoints](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-hourly-or-processing-charge), and the endpoint keeps the instance uploads off the internet.

options.text: Create an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon S3, with an endpoint network interface in a private subnet in each Availability Zone.
options.why: One endpoint per zone is private too, but an interface endpoint is [billed for each hour that your interface VPC endpoint is provisioned in each Availability Zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-interface-endpoint-billed-hour-per-az-and-gb).

options.text: Create an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 in each Availability Zone, and add a second NAT gateway so that each zone has its own.
options.why: The endpoint plus a second NAT gateway works, but the interface endpoint and the extra NAT gateway add hourly charges that the uploads do not need.

options.text: Move the instances to public subnets, assign public IP addresses, and send the uploads to Amazon S3 through an internet gateway.
options.why: An internet gateway sends the uploads over the internet, so the uploads do not reach Amazon S3 privately.

items.explanation: Both endpoint types keep the uploads private, so the word privately does not decide. The cost qualifier does: [there are no data processing or hourly charges for using Gateway Type VPC endpoints](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-hourly-or-processing-charge), and routing the uploads through the gateway endpoint lets the company [avoid the NAT Gateway Data Processing charge](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-hourly-or-processing-charge).
items.takeaway: Private is a requirement that both endpoints meet; the cost qualifier then picks the gateway endpoint.
items.twin: If the stem said "servers in the company's data center" instead: an interface endpoint, because [gateway endpoints do not allow access from on-premises networks, from peered VPCs in other AWS Regions, or through a transit gateway](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-onprem-cross-region-tgw).
items.say: Both endpoints are private, but the gateway endpoint for S3 has no hourly charge, so it wins on cost.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the MOST cost-effective solution that meets every requirement.

I mark the constraints: the uploads go to Amazon S3 in the same Region, they come only from the instances in the VPC, they must reach Amazon S3 privately, and the NAT gateway data processing charge is the cost to cut.
Before I look at the options, I predict a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3, because it keeps the traffic off the internet and has no hourly or data processing charge.

I remove the move to public subnets, because an internet gateway sends the uploads over the internet. I remove the option with a second NAT gateway, because it adds a charge that the uploads do not need.

Between the gateway endpoint and the interface endpoint the difference is cost; the stem says the uploads come only from the instances in the VPC, so both endpoints work, and the gateway endpoint has no hourly charge.
Check: the gateway endpoint meets every constraint and removes the NAT gateway data processing charge for the uploads. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: Add a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 and route the private subnets' S3 prefix list to it; it is private, has no hourly or data processing charge, and removes the NAT gateway from the path.

items.stem: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets in two Availability Zones. The instances call a partner's API on the internet. A small team operates the AWS environment and does not want to patch or replace network devices. The instances must not have public IP addresses, and internet access for the instances must be highly available. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Launch a NAT instance in a public subnet in each Availability Zone, and run a script that moves the routes to a healthy NAT instance after a failure.
options.why: It works, but a NAT instance is [managed by you, for example, by installing software updates or operating system patches on the instance](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-vs-instance-maintenance), which the team wants to avoid.

options.text: Attach an internet gateway to the VPC, assign a public IP address to each instance, and route the private subnets to the internet gateway.
options.why: The stem forbids public IP addresses on the instances, so a route to an internet gateway breaks a stated requirement.
options.misconception: drops the NAT device by breaking the requirement against public IP addresses

options.text: Create a gateway VPC endpoint, add it to the route table of each private subnet, and send the partner API traffic to the endpoint.
options.why: [Gateway VPC endpoints provide reliable connectivity to Amazon S3 and DynamoDB without requiring an internet gateway or a NAT device for your VPC](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-s3-dynamodb-no-privatelink); a partner API is not one of them.
options.misconception: uses an endpoint for Amazon S3 and DynamoDB to reach an API on the internet

options.text: Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet in each Availability Zone, and route each private subnet to the NAT gateway in its own zone.
options.why: A NAT gateway is [managed by AWS](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-vs-instance-maintenance), and [NAT gateways provide better availability, higher bandwidth, and requires less administrative effort](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-preferred-over-nat-instance).

items.explanation: Two options give the instances highly available internet access without public IP addresses: NAT gateways, and NAT instances with a failover script. The qualifier ranks them. A NAT instance needs you to [use a script to manage failover between instances](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-vs-instance-availability) and to patch it, while a NAT gateway is [managed by AWS](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-vs-instance-maintenance).
items.takeaway: A small team and LEAST operational overhead: choose the managed device over the one you patch.
items.twin: If the stem said "the instances call Amazon S3" instead: a gateway endpoint, because [Gateway VPC endpoints provide reliable connectivity to Amazon S3 and DynamoDB without requiring an internet gateway or a NAT device for your VPC](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-s3-dynamodb-no-privatelink).
items.say: Both work, but a NAT gateway is managed by AWS, so the small team has nothing to patch.

solvers.stem_only: Use managed NAT gateways, one in a public subnet in each Availability Zone, with each private subnet routed to the NAT gateway in its own zone; no patching and zone-independent.

items.stem: A company runs workloads on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets in three Availability Zones of one VPC. Each private subnet has its own route table. The instances download software updates from a vendor's website on the internet, and the traffic volume is small. The instances must not have public IP addresses. Internet access must continue if one Availability Zone fails. What is the MOST cost-effective solution that meets these requirements?
keywords: Internet access must continue if one Availability Zone fails

options.text: Create one NAT gateway in a public subnet in one Availability Zone, and point the default route of every private route table to that NAT gateway.
options.why: One gateway in one zone is the cheapest, but if its zone fails, [resources in the other Availability Zones lose internet access](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-shared-across-azs-loses-internet), which breaks the requirement.

options.text: Create one NAT gateway in a public subnet in each Availability Zone, and point the default route of each private route table to the NAT gateway in its zone.
options.why: AWS says to [deploy a NAT gateway in each active AZ](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-each-active-az-in-production) in production, so each zone keeps internet access when another zone fails.

options.text: Create two NAT gateways in public subnets in each Availability Zone, and point the default route of each private route table to one NAT gateway in its zone.
options.why: It works, but [each NAT gateway is created in a specific Availability Zone and implemented with redundancy in that zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-one-az-redundant-in-zone), so a second one adds cost.

options.text: Assign a public IP address to each instance, and point the default route of each private route table to the internet gateway of the VPC.
options.why: The stem forbids public IP addresses on the instances, so this design breaks a stated requirement at any price.

items.explanation: The stem requires internet access to continue when one zone fails. A shared gateway is the cheapest design, but it breaks that requirement, so it is removed before the qualifier ranks. Of the designs that work, one gateway in each zone costs less than two, because NAT gateways are [charged depending on the number of NAT gateways you use, duration of usage, and amount of data that you send through the NAT gateways](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-vs-instance-cost).
items.takeaway: A hard requirement removes the cheapest design first; then the qualifier ranks what is left.
items.twin: If the stem said "an interruption of internet access is acceptable" instead: one shared NAT gateway, because the designs with more gateways cost more and the interruption is allowed.
items.say: Internet access must survive a zone failure, so each zone gets its own NAT gateway.

solvers.stem_only: One NAT gateway in a public subnet in each of the three Availability Zones, each private route table pointing to the NAT gateway in its own zone; this is the cheapest design that survives a zone failure.

items.stem: A company runs a reporting application on Amazon EC2 instances. The application reads objects from one Amazon S3 bucket by using the access key of an IAM user. The key is stored in a configuration file on each instance. A new company policy requires that no long-term credentials are stored on the instances and that the application has least privilege. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: no long-term credentials are stored on the instances

options.text: Run a scheduled script that rotates the access key of the IAM user every week and copies the new key into the file on each instance.
options.why: A rotated key is still an access key, and access keys [remain valid until you manually revoke them](../facts/iam.md#iam-long-term-keys-valid-until-revoked-temporary-expire).
options.misconception: believes that a rotated access key is no longer a long-term credential

options.text: Create an IAM role with a policy that allows read actions on the objects in that one bucket, and let Amazon EC2 assume the role.
options.why: A role [does not have standard long-term credentials, such as a password or access keys](../facts/iam.md#iam-users-have-long-term-credentials-roles-do-not), and one bucket keeps least privilege.

options.text: Create an IAM role with the AdministratorAccess managed policy, so that the application keeps working when it later needs other AWS services.
options.why: AdministratorAccess gives far more than reading one bucket, and least privilege means [defining the actions that can be taken on specific resources under specific conditions](../facts/iam.md#iam-best-practice-least-privilege-definition).

options.text: Attach the role to the instances through an instance profile, and delete the access key and the configuration file from each instance.
options.why: Through the instance profile, [AWS delivers the temporary credentials of an IAM role to that compute resource](../facts/iam.md#iam-compute-services-receive-role-credentials-no-keys-needed), so the stored key can go.

options.text: Create a separate IAM role for each instance, each with its own copy of the read policy, and attach each role to its own instance.
options.why: It works, but one shared role serves every instance, and a change to that role [propagates to all of them](../facts/iam.md#iam-ec2-role-credentials-rotate-automatically); separate roles multiply the work.

items.explanation: Each correct step is right on its own, and the two work together. The role replaces the stored key, and role credentials on EC2 are [temporary and updated automatically](../facts/iam.md#iam-ec2-role-credentials-rotate-automatically), so the team does not rotate or store them.
items.takeaway: Judge each option alone, then check that the chosen steps work together as one solution.
items.twin: If the stem said "the application runs as an AWS Lambda function" instead: the function's execution role, because [AWS delivers the temporary credentials of an IAM role to that compute resource](../facts/iam.md#iam-compute-services-receive-role-credentials-no-keys-needed).
items.say: Create a least-privilege role and attach it through an instance profile, then delete the stored key.

solvers.stem_only: Create one IAM role with a policy scoped to read objects in that single bucket and a trust policy for Amazon EC2, attach it to the instances through an instance profile, and remove the stored access key.

items.stem: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets in two Availability Zones. The instances currently send large uploads to an Amazon S3 bucket in the same AWS Region through one NAT gateway. The uploads also come from servers in the company's data center, which connect to the VPC over an AWS Direct Connect private virtual interface. All uploads must reach Amazon S3 privately through the VPC, and the company wants to reduce the NAT gateway data processing charges. What is the MOST cost-effective solution that meets these requirements?
keywords: also come from servers in the company's data center

options.text: Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3, and add a route to the endpoint in the route table of each private subnet.
options.why: It is the cheapest, but [gateway endpoints do not allow access from on-premises networks, from peered VPCs in other AWS Regions, or through a transit gateway](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-onprem-cross-region-tgw).

options.text: Create an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon S3, with an endpoint network interface in a private subnet in each Availability Zone.
options.why: An interface endpoint [supports connectivity over Direct Connect](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-faq-interface-endpoints-privatelink), so the data center servers and the instances both reach Amazon S3 privately.

options.text: Create an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 in each Availability Zone, and add a second NAT gateway so that each zone has its own.
options.why: The endpoint plus a second NAT gateway works, but the extra NAT gateway adds an hourly charge that the private uploads do not need.

options.text: Move the instances to public subnets, assign public IP addresses, and send the uploads to Amazon S3 through an internet gateway.
options.why: An internet gateway sends the uploads over the internet, so the uploads do not reach Amazon S3 privately.

items.explanation: The cheapest endpoint fails one requirement, because [gateway endpoints do not allow access from on-premises networks, from peered VPCs in other AWS Regions, or through a transit gateway](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-onprem-cross-region-tgw). For that case [you must use an interface endpoint, which is available for an additional cost](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-onprem-cross-region-tgw). The qualifier then ranks what is left, and the interface endpoint without an extra NAT gateway costs least.
items.takeaway: The cheapest option is out when it fails one requirement; then rank the options that remain.
items.twin: If the stem said "come only from the instances in the VPC" instead: a gateway endpoint, because [there are no data processing or hourly charges for using Gateway Type VPC endpoints](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-gateway-endpoint-no-hourly-or-processing-charge).
items.say: The data center also uploads, and a gateway endpoint does not serve on-premises traffic, so I'd use an interface endpoint.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the MOST cost-effective solution that meets every requirement.

I mark the constraints: the uploads come from the instances and from servers in the data center over a Direct Connect private virtual interface, they must reach Amazon S3 privately through the VPC, and the NAT gateway data processing charge is the cost to cut.
Before I look at the options, I predict a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3, because it has no hourly or data processing charge.

I remove the move to public subnets, because an internet gateway sends the uploads over the internet. I remove the option with a second NAT gateway, because it adds a charge that the uploads do not need.

Between the gateway endpoint and the interface endpoint the difference is who can use the endpoint. My first idea breaks because gateway endpoints do not allow access from on-premises networks, and the stem says the data center also uploads. So I choose the interface endpoint, which supports connectivity over Direct Connect.
Check: the interface endpoint meets every constraint for both sources of uploads, and it removes the NAT gateway charge for them. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: The deciding constraint is that uploads from the data center over the Direct Connect private VIF must also reach S3 privately through the VPC. A gateway endpoint for S3 is free but cannot be used from on-premises networks, so it fails that requirement. An interface VPC endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) for S3, with an endpoint network interface in each AZ, serves both the EC2 instances and the on-premises servers privately and removes the NAT gateway data processing charges. No extra NAT gateway and no public subnets are needed.

items.stem: A company runs Linux applications on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets of a VPC in one AWS Region. Administrators connect to the instances a few times each week to troubleshoot problems. The security team wants to avoid any inbound SSH access from the internet to the VPC. Every administrator session must also be recorded and kept for audit. Which solution will meet these requirements?
keywords: wants to avoid any inbound SSH access
must also be recorded and kept for audit

options.text: Launch a bastion host in a public subnet, allow port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0 to the bastion, and connect through it to the instances.
options.why: The bastion accepts SSH from the internet, which is the inbound access that the security team wants to avoid.
options.misconception: believes that a bastion host makes SSH from the internet acceptable

options.text: Add a security group rule that allows port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0 to each instance, and turn on VPC Flow Logs for the subnets.
options.why: Logging does not stop the access: the rule still opens SSH from the internet, which the security team wants to avoid.

options.text: Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager to open sessions to the instances, and send the session logs to Amazon S3 or CloudWatch Logs.
options.why: Well-Architected says to [use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager to provide interactive access to instances when necessary](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-wa-sec06-no-ssh-rdp-use-session-manager), with session logs for audit.

options.text: Add a network ACL rule that allows port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0 to the private subnets, and keep the shell history on each instance.
options.why: A network ACL allow rule still opens SSH from the internet, and a shell history on the instance is not a session record.
options.misconception: believes that a network ACL rule is a safer way to open SSH

items.explanation: The phrase "wants to avoid any inbound SSH access" removes every option that opens SSH. Well-Architected guidance is that ingress rules [do not permit access on port 22/tcp (SSH) or port 3389/tcp (RDP)](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-wa-sec06-no-ssh-rdp-use-session-manager), and that teams [use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager to provide interactive access to instances when necessary](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-wa-sec06-no-ssh-rdp-use-session-manager). Session Manager can log each session to Amazon S3 or CloudWatch Logs.
items.takeaway: A wants-to-avoid requirement removes options before anything else; then check what is left.
items.twin: If the stem said "Windows instances that administrators reach with RDP" instead: still Session Manager, because ingress rules [do not permit access on port 22/tcp (SSH) or port 3389/tcp (RDP)](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-wa-sec06-no-ssh-rdp-use-session-manager).
items.say: They want no inbound SSH and a record of every session, so I'd use Session Manager with session logging.

solvers.stem_only: Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager with no inbound ports open, and enable session logging to Amazon S3 or CloudWatch Logs for audit.

items.stem: A company runs a web application on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets behind an Application Load Balancer in public subnets. The load balancer and the instances have separate security groups. The security team must block one abusive public IP address range in the subnets of the load balancer. The team must also ensure that the instances accept HTTPS traffic from the load balancer only and restrict all other inbound traffic. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: block one abusive public IP address range
accept HTTPS traffic from the load balancer only

options.text: Add an inbound deny rule for the address range to the network ACL of the load balancer's subnets, with a lower rule number than the allow rules.
options.why: Network ACL rules are evaluated [starting with the lowest numbered rule](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-nacl-rule-order-first-match), so the deny rule stops the range before an allow rule matches.

options.text: Add an inbound deny rule for the address range to the security group of the load balancer, and keep its existing allow rule for HTTPS.
options.why: A deny rule in the security group cannot exist: in a security group, [you can specify allow rules, but not deny rules](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-allow-rules-only).
options.misconception: believes that a security group can hold deny rules

options.text: Add an inbound deny rule for the address range to the network ACL of every subnet in the VPC, and repeat the rule for each new subnet.
options.why: A deny rule in every subnet's network ACL works, but the team maintains it everywhere, although the traffic enters through the load balancer's subnets.

options.text: Change the security group of the instances to allow HTTPS from 0.0.0.0/0, and rely on the network ACL rule to stop the abusive range.
options.why: An allow rule from 0.0.0.0/0 lets any address reach the instances on HTTPS, which breaks the second requirement of the stem.
options.misconception: believes that the network ACL rule also limits the instances to load balancer traffic

options.text: Change the security group of the instances to allow HTTPS from the security group of the load balancer, and remove all other inbound rules.
options.why: As in the AWS example, the instance security group [allows inbound HTTPS access from the load balancer](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-chain-web-allows-lb-sg) by naming the load balancer's security group.

items.explanation: Two requirements need two steps, and each correct option meets one of them on its own. Blocking an address range needs a deny rule, and [network ACLs can be used to set both Allow and Deny rules](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-sg-allow-rules-only). Limiting the instances to load balancer traffic is a security group rule that names the security group of the load balancer.
items.takeaway: Two requirements, two steps: each correct option meets one requirement on its own.
items.twin: If the stem said "allow HTTPS from one partner address range" instead: an allow rule in the security group, because that stem needs no deny rule.
items.say: A deny for a range goes in the network ACL, and the instances allow HTTPS from the load balancer's security group.

solvers.stem_only: Block the range with an inbound deny rule in the network ACL of the load balancer's subnets (security groups cannot deny), numbered before the allow rules; and set the instance security group to allow HTTPS only from the load balancer's security group.

items.stem: A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled and has 40 member accounts. Each member account sends VPC flow logs to a central log archive. Administrators in the member accounts have full IAM permissions in their own accounts. The security team must ensure that no one in the member accounts, including the root user, can delete the flow logs of their VPCs. The team wants to centrally manage this control. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule in each member account that sends an alert to the security team when someone deletes a flow log.
options.why: An alert reports a deletion after it happens, but the stem asks for a control that stops the deletion itself.

options.text: Attach an identity-based policy that denies the deletion of flow logs to every IAM user and every IAM role in the member accounts.
options.why: Administrators can detach the policy, and you [cannot attach identity-based policies to the root user](../facts/iam.md#iam-root-user-no-identity-policies-or-boundary).
options.misconception: believes that an identity-based deny binds administrators and the root user

options.text: Create an SCP that denies the deletion of flow logs, and attach the SCP to each member account in the organization one account at a time.
options.why: Attaching the SCP account by account works, but it is more work than one attachment at the root of the organization.

options.text: Create an SCP that denies the deletion of flow logs, and attach the SCP once to the root of the organization in AWS Organizations.
options.why: Attached [to the root of your organization](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-faq-attach-at-root-ou-or-account), the SCP reaches every member account and restricts principals [including the member account's root user](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-applies-to-member-root-user).

items.explanation: The stem asks for a control that stops the deletion, and the strongest principal in the stem is the root user. An SCP [restricts permissions for IAM users and roles in member accounts](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-applies-to-member-root-user), [including the member account's root user](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-applies-to-member-root-user), and member principals [cannot remove or change SCPs that are applied to that account](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-faq-member-principals-cannot-change-scps). Attached [to the root of your organization](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-faq-attach-at-root-ou-or-account), one SCP covers every member account.
items.takeaway: When the stem forbids an action for every principal, root user included, choose a deny SCP, not an alert or an IAM policy.
items.twin: If the stem said "wants to be notified when someone deletes a flow log" instead: the EventBridge alert, because that stem asks for detection, not prevention.
items.say: Nobody, not even the root user, can be allowed to delete the logs, so I'd attach a deny SCP to the organization root.

solvers.stem_only: Create a service control policy that denies ec2:DeleteFlowLogs and attach it once at the organization root so it applies to all member accounts, including their root users.

items.stem: A company runs a production web application on Amazon EC2 instances in one Availability Zone of an AWS Region. The instances sit in private subnets behind an Application Load Balancer and reach the internet through one NAT gateway in the same zone. The application and its outbound internet access must keep working if one Availability Zone fails. Recovery in another Region is not required. Which combination of steps is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
keywords: must keep working if one Availability Zone fails
Recovery in another Region is not required

options.text: Launch the instances in an Auto Scaling group across private subnets in two Availability Zones, and register the group with the load balancer.
options.why: Instances in two zones keep serving when one zone fails, as AWS advises with [at least two Availability Zones (AZs) in a Region](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-production-at-least-two-azs).

options.text: Copy the whole stack to a second Region, and use Amazon Route 53 failover routing to send users to the second Region after a failure.
options.why: It works, but AWS names this anti-pattern: [you implement a multi-Region architecture when a multi-AZ architecture would satisfy business requirements](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-multi-region-when-multi-az-suffices-is-anti-pattern).

options.text: Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet in the second Availability Zone, and route each private subnet to the NAT gateway in its zone.
options.why: AWS advises you to [create a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone, and configure your routing to ensure that resources use the NAT gateway in the same Availability Zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-shared-across-azs-loses-internet).

options.text: Keep the one NAT gateway, and route the private subnets of both Availability Zones to that NAT gateway in the first Availability Zone.
options.why: If the first zone fails, [resources in the other Availability Zones lose internet access](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-shared-across-azs-loses-internet), so outbound access breaks.

options.text: Replace the instances with larger instance types in the same Availability Zone, so that each instance can carry the full load alone.
options.why: Larger instances stay in one zone, and if that zone fails, [none of your EC2 instances would be available](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-single-az-failure-takes-all-instances).

items.explanation: The stem names the failure of one Availability Zone and does not require another Region. [Deploying your workload across multiple Availability Zones in an AWS Region is part of a high availability strategy](../facts/well-architected.md#well-architected-multi-az-is-ha-and-dr-multi-region-active-passive), so instances and NAT gateways in two zones survive that failure. A second Region costs more than the requirement asks.
items.takeaway: A zone failure needs two zones; a second Region is more than the stem asks for.
items.twin: If the stem said "must keep working if the whole Region fails" instead: the copy in a second Region, because each Region is [designed to be isolated from the other Regions](../facts/global-infrastructure.md#global-infrastructure-region-isolated-for-fault-tolerance).
items.say: The stem names a zone failure, so two zones with a NAT gateway each is enough, and a second Region costs more.

solvers.stem_only: Run the instances in an Auto Scaling group across private subnets in two Availability Zones behind the load balancer, and add a NAT gateway in the second zone with each private subnet routed to the NAT gateway in its own zone; no multi-Region setup.
